title: Is English really a Germanic language?

entries.note: A branch of the Indo-European family descended from [[from:Proto-Germanic]], split into [[see:West Germanic]], [[see:North Germanic]] and [[see:East Germanic]]; English counts as Germanic despite its many Latinate words.
The reconstructed common ancestor of the Germanic languages, spoken in Iron Age Scandinavia, northern Germany and the North Sea and Baltic coasts; it underwent [[see:Grimm's law]].
The Germanic branch including English, German, Dutch, Afrikaans, Frisian, Yiddish, Low Saxon and Scots; it divides further into high and low varieties.
The Scandinavian branch of Germanic: Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Icelandic, Faroese and others.
The now-extinct Germanic branch, which included [[see:Gothic]].
The best-attested East Germanic language in writing.
Undeniably Germanic, with three genders and four cases like German; brought by the [[see:Anglo-Saxons]] from the fifth century and written in [[see:runes]].
Swedish for I am hungry, whose verb är is related to English [[same-root:are]].
Borrowed from the Vikings' Old Norse and related to the Swedish är in [[same-root:jag är hungrig]].
The Germanic settlers, [[see:Angles]], [[see:Saxons]] and [[see:Jutes]], who introduced [[see:Old English]] to Britain from the fifth century.
One of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain from the mid fifth century, bringing West Germanic dialects that became [[see:Old English]].
One of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain from the mid fifth century, bringing West Germanic dialects that became [[see:Old English]].
One of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain from the mid fifth century, bringing West Germanic dialects that became [[see:Old English]].
Germanic dialects from lower altitudes; the Anglo-Saxons spoke them, English and Dutch count as low, and Low German dialects survive in Germany. Contrasts with [[see:High German]].
Named for the altitude of southern Germany, not for being further north; it is modern standard German, the dominant dialect.
Entered English in the Viking age, 8th to 11th centuries, often displacing native Old English words; [[see:Icelandic]] best preserves what it was like.
The region of eastern and northern England the Danes received in a deal with an Anglo-Saxon kingdom; it includes [[see:Derby]].
Rob's home town in the Danelaw, a Viking place name ending in [[from:-by]].
Place names ending in -by are Old Norse in origin, found along a strip down the east of England.
The Viking army led by [[see:Ivar the Boneless]], active before the Danelaw was established.
Leader of the [[see:Great Heathen Army]], known from the Vikings TV series as the son of [[see:Ragnar Lothbrok]].
An Old Norse word, also meaning cloud, that displaced the Old English [[see:heaven]] in this sense.
The Old English word for sky, replaced by Norse [[see:sky]] but still used in other contexts.
An Old Norse word that replaced the Old English [[see:seax]].
A Germanic short sword; the Old English word was displaced by Norse [[see:knife]].
Old Norse, literally wind eye; it replaced an Old English word meaning eyehole, and the hosts have discussed it before.
Borrowed from Old Norse, possibly as a euphemism; it displaced the Old English verb that became [[see:starve]].
Once the general English word for dying, related to German [[same-root:sterben]], it narrowed to dying from lack of food once Norse [[see:die]] took over.
German for to die, directly related to English [[same-root:starve]]; the word is missing from the captions.
An Old English verb for dying, used more often than the predecessor of [[see:starve]] until Norse [[see:die]] took over.
An Old English way of saying to die, possibly euphemistic, before Old Norse [[see:die]] took over.
Old English for to cease living, literally to go or ride forth.
Taken from the Vikings, like Scandinavian taka; West Germanic German and Dutch instead use words like [[see:nehmen]]. Ultimately shares a root with [[same-root:tackle]].
German (and Dutch nemen) for to take; these West Germanic languages have no word like English [[see:take]].
An entirely Viking phrase, since [[see:they]], [[see:are]], [[see:take]], [[see:their]] and [[see:egg]] all come from Old Norse.
Borrowed from the Vikings.
A pronoun from the Vikings; it spared English from using [[see:him]] as a plural, and singular they is perfectly natural.
A pronoun borrowed from the Vikings.
A pronoun borrowed from the Vikings, replacing Old English plural [[see:him]].
Via Middle Dutch from the root of [[same-root:take]]; first meant any rigging, something to grasp, then fishing gear, and also tackling someone in football.
West Germanic languages use speak and its relatives, while North Germanic ones use words related to [[see:talk]] or [[see:snakke]].
Related to the usual North Germanic words for speaking, which English uses [[see:speak]] for.
Norwegian for to talk, related to [[same-root:snack]] through moving the mouth up and down, so I speak Norwegian becomes I snack Norwegian.
Related to Norwegian [[same-root:snakke]], to talk, both about moving the mouth.
Preserves the Old Norse infinitive particle [[from:at]], so it means at do, much like [[equivalent:to-do]]; a vestige of Norse grammar.
The Norse infinitive particle, equivalent to English infinitive to, surviving in [[gave:ado]] and in Swedish att.
A big to-do means the same as a big [[equivalent:ado]], made with the English infinitive particle.
Vikings who settled in France; the French brought by [[see:William the Conqueror]] in 1066 was a Germanic-sounding variety, full of [[see:Frankish]] words.
Brought the Germanic-influenced French of the [[see:Normans]] to England in 1066.
A West Germanic language spoken in what is now France; it gave English words like [[gave:warden]], [[gave:guardian]] and [[gave:heinous]] indirectly through French and Latin.
From [[from:Frankish]], from an idea of directing your gaze; one of a Norman and central French couplet with [[same-root:guardian]].
From [[from:Frankish]], from an idea of directing your gaze; one of a Norman and central French couplet with [[same-root:warden]].
Said to come from a [[from:Frankish]] word meaning lump or bump; the word is unclear in the captions.
From a [[from:Frankish]] root meaning hate.
Paired with [[same-root:warranty]] as a G and W couplet from Norman versus central French, like [[see:warden]] and [[see:guardian]].
Paired with [[same-root:guarantee]] as a W and G couplet from Norman versus central French.
Listed among the G and W couplets from Norman versus central French; its partner is garbled in the captions.
A W couplet partner of French [[same-root:gaufre]].
The French for a waffle, the G counterpart of English [[same-root:waffle]].
Seventeenth-century wars during which English sailors and merchants borrowed many Dutch nautical terms such as [[see:skipper]] and [[see:yacht]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
A nautical term borrowed from Dutch around the 17th-century [[see:Anglo-Dutch Wars]].
Bravery from alcohol, one of the expressions where [[see:Dutch]] became an insulting label for things seen as foreign or morally suspect.
Splitting the bill so each person pays for themselves; one of the mocking English uses of [[see:Dutch]].
Shoddy workmanship; another disparaging English use of [[see:Dutch]].
A historical English name for syphilis, a slight on an enemy like the English uses of [[see:Dutch]].

Closely related to [[same-root:Deutsch]]; originally meant Germanic speaker generally, not specifically from the Netherlands, hence [[see:High Dutch]], [[see:Low Dutch]] and [[see:Pennsylvania Dutch]].
What Germans call themselves and their language, a unifying name for the confederated states' shared language; related to English [[same-root:Dutch]].
No more Germanic than other Germanic languages; it resembles [[unrelated:Germanic]] only because English chose the word [[see:Germany]].
Rob calls it a stupid English name, causing confusion with Germanic; Germans call their country [[see:Deutschland]].
The Germans' own name for their country, from [[from:Deutsch]].
Once meant German, while [[see:Low Dutch]] meant Netherlandish.
Once meant Netherlandish, while [[see:High Dutch]] meant German.
Actually German: descendants of German-speaking settlers from the Rhineland and Switzerland, whose word [[from:Deutsch]] was reworked by English speakers as [[see:Dutch]].
Rob's tongue-in-cheek proposal for an English name for Germany, alongside [[see:Netherlandic]] for the people of the Netherlands.
Rob's proposed name for the people of the Netherlands, freeing [[see:Dutchland]] for Germany.
The consonant shift that set [[see:Proto-Germanic]] apart, turning P into F and K into H; named after [[see:Jacob Grimm]], as shown by [[see:father]] versus [[see:pater]].
One of the [[see:Brothers Grimm]], who outlined the consonant shift known as [[see:Grimm's law]].
Jacob and Wilhelm, fairy tale collectors who gathered the tales partly to analyse their language.
Latin for dog; its K sound corresponds to the H of Germanic [[same-root:hound]] under [[see:Grimm's law]].
The standard Germanic dog word, hund or hound, whose H corresponds to the C of Latin [[same-root:canis]].
The same word as Latin [[same-root:pater]], with P to F and T to TH under [[see:Grimm's law]], showing English is Germanic.
Latin for father, directly related to English [[same-root:father]] before the [[see:Grimm's law]] shift.
Taken from non-Germanic languages; contrasted with [[same-root:one horn]] and German [[equivalent:Einhorn]] to show the C to H shift.
The Germanic counterpart of [[same-root:unicorn]], showing the C to H shift.
Contrasted with [[same-root:horn of plenty]] to show the C to H shift.
The Germanic counterpart of [[same-root:cornucopia]], showing the C to H shift.
German for [[equivalent:unicorn]], literally one horn, a typically Germanic compound like English [[see:toothbrush]] or [[see:skyscraper]].
An example of English making words by joining two words, a very Germanic habit.
An example of the Germanic habit of compounding.
An example of the Germanic habit of compounding.
An example of the Germanic habit of compounding.
An example of the Germanic habit of compounding.
Its Germanic word order contrasts with the Italian, Spanish and French equivalents, which say scrape sky.
Latin counterpart of [[same-root:lip]], showing the B to P shift under [[see:Grimm's law]].
Shows the Germanic shift of B to P compared with Latin [[same-root:labium]].
Latin counterpart of [[same-root:ten]], showing the D to T shift.
Shows the Germanic D to T shift compared with Latin [[same-root:decem]].
Latin counterpart of [[same-root:knee]], showing the G to K shift.
Shows the Germanic G to K shift compared with Latin [[same-root:genu]].
Partly attributed to the Germanic habit of stressing first syllables, which reduced unstressed syllables.
A French borrowing stressed on the second syllable, showing that English stress can't be predicted from the Germanic first-syllable rule.
A Germanic vowel change where vowels moved toward an I or E sound, producing [[see:foot]] and feet, [[see:mouse]] and mice; linked to [[see:umlaut]].
Its plural feet comes from [[see:i-mutation]], paralleling the German umlauted plural of the same word.
Its plural mice is an example of [[see:i-mutation]].
Both the two dots over a vowel and the phenomenon of vowel change German uses in plurals, which Old English shared, as in [[see:foot]] and feet.
The ten-dollar word for building tenses like the future with helper words, as Germanic languages do.
English alone uses will for the future; in most other Germanic languages its relatives are the standard word for [[see:want]], meaning to will something to be.
Based on the idea of lacking something, unlike the [[see:will]]-type words other Germanic languages use.
Unlike other Germanic languages' scribe-type words, it relates to fashioning things, like [[same-root:wright]].
Connected with [[same-root:write]] through the idea of fashioning something.
From an Old English word for being advised or taking advice, unlike the L words such as German [[see:lesen]]; discussed in a recent episode.
One of the Germanic L words for reading that contrast with English [[see:read]].
The Germanic script, made of straight lines for scratching, in which Old English was written; Rob has made a whole video on them.
A rune for the TH sound, curled to fit the Latin alphabet; it looked like a P over a B, and Icelandic still uses it.
A rune for the W sound that looked too much like a P, confusing readers of [[see:Beowulf]], and was replaced by double U.
Hard to read partly because it is full of [[see:wynn]] letters that look like Ps.
Still used with [[see:thorn]] in Icelandic for the voiced TH sound, though the two letters are partly interchangeable.
A remote, conservative language that best shows what Old Norse was like; it keeps [[see:thorn]] and [[see:eth]], and three genders and four cases.
The push to keep English free of foreign, especially classical, borrowings, as in [[see:Anglish]] and the [[see:Inkhorn Controversy]].
A tongue-in-cheek modern movement replacing non-Germanic English words with Germanic equivalents; Rob made a video about it.
Better intended than [[see:Anglish]]: it avoids rare words and needless euphemisms, some Latin-derived, and has drawn on [[see:George Orwell]].
Needlessly complex Greek and Latin borrowings; an inkhorn was a scholar's portable horn inkwell, or the words were so long you had to keep redipping.
A 16th–17th-century debate on classical borrowing: [[see:Thomas Elyot]] and [[see:George Pettie]] favoured it, while [[see:Thomas Wilson]] and [[see:John Cheke]] opposed it.
Favoured extensive Latin borrowing to enrich English in the [[see:Inkhorn Controversy]].
Favoured extensive Latin borrowing in the [[see:Inkhorn Controversy]].
Opposed classical borrowings; [[see:inkhorn terms]] appeared in his The Art of Rhetoric.
Wanted English kept pure and unmangled, and tried to rewrite the Bible without Latinate or Greek terms.
A purist replacement proposed by opponents of [[see:inkhorn terms]] for knowledge; Rob later uses it himself.
A 19th-century polyglot who proposed reviving Germanic strong old Anglo-Saxon speech so non-classically educated speakers could understand; author of [[see:An Outline of English Speechcraft]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s book listing Germanic replacements for classical words, such as [[see:speechcraft]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for [[see:grammar]].
Barnes called it a misused word: from Greek grapho, to write, it means a writing, and Greek [[from:grammatica]] meant book lore, not speech teaching.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for flexible.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for meteor, built on [[from:welkin]].
From the Old English for cloud or sky; part of Barnes's [[gave:welkinfire]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for democracy.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement, alongside word building, for etymology; Rob loves it.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for astronomy.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for chronology.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for ornithology.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for botany.
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for chemistry, ironic since matter itself is Latin-derived.
Now tacked onto everything, especially by YA fantasy fans, making Barnes seem ahead of his time with coinages like [[see:star lore]].
[[see:William Barnes]]'s replacement for aphorism, which Jess reads as calling them brainless clichés.
In the 1940s he called words like [[see:ameliorate]], [[see:extraneous]] and [[see:clandestine]] needlessly Latinate, fuelling the [[see:Plain English movement]].
Called needlessly Latinate by [[see:George Orwell]].
Called needlessly Latinate by [[see:George Orwell]].
Called needlessly Latinate by [[see:George Orwell]].
Said he preferred short Anglo-Saxon words; his [[see:We Shall Fight on the Beaches]] speech relies heavily on them.

entries.note: [[see:Winston Churchill]]'s speech, mostly short Anglo-Saxon words; in one section the only Latin-derived word is [[see:surrender]].
The only Latin-derived word in one section of [[see:We Shall Fight on the Beaches]].
An Old English compound meaning to stand among something, since [[from:under]] is related to inter; you are immersed within the subject.
Originally related to inter, meaning among, which explains [[gave:understand]].
German for to support, literally being underneath something, compared with [[see:understand]].
Old English for to examine or closely investigate, literally to seek among things.
Old English for to think critically or consider carefully, literally to think between or among.
Old English for receiving something from someone, literally taking between two people.
A prefixed verb English still uses, though it means something different from go under.
An Old English plural pronoun replaced by Norse [[see:they]] and [[see:them]]; Rob is glad English doesn't still use it as a plural.
All Germanic languages have unique words for 11 and [[see:twelve]] instead of one-teen, perhaps because twelve mattered, possibly from counting finger segments.
Like [[see:eleven]] it has its own word in all Germanic languages, suggesting twelve was once important to Germanic peoples.
Base-20 counting, found in Danish, Celtic languages and French [[see:four twenties]]; Jess finds the word endlessly funny. The word is missing from the captions.
How French expresses 80, an example of base-20 [[see:vigesimal]] counting.
A daughter of Dutch developed in South Africa, very different from other Germanic languages; source of [[gave:apartheid]], [[gave:aardvark]] and [[gave:trek]].
From [[from:Afrikaans]], ultimately Dutch, meaning separateness.
An animal name from [[from:Afrikaans]] meaning earth pig.
From [[from:Afrikaans]], literally tree snake; a very venomous tree snake.
Open grassland, a word from [[from:Afrikaans]].
Originally Dutch for to draw or pull, entering English in the 1850s via [[from:Afrikaans]]; related to [[same-root:drag]], [[same-root:track]] and [[same-root:train]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
A modern German borrowing meaning children garden.
A modern borrowing from German, where it meant dumpling or noodle; German now calls pasta [[see:Nudeln]].
German for pasta generally, even spaghetti, which annoys Rob; related to English [[same-root:noodle]].
A German borrowing meaning double walker or double-goer.
A German borrowing meaning knocking or noisy ghost, discussed in an earlier episode; shares its geist with [[same-root:zeitgeist]].
A German borrowing meaning time spirit, with the same geist as [[same-root:poltergeist]].
An obvious modern borrowing from Norwegian.
A modern Scandinavian borrowing for ice.
From Norwegian, naming the little planktonic crustaceans.
A modern Scandinavian borrowing.
A modern Scandinavian borrowing.
A modern Scandinavian borrowing.
A West Germanic language close enough to German to be partly understood; many seemingly German English words, like [[gave:mensch]], came via Yiddish and New York slang.
A good guy; borrowed from [[from:Yiddish]], probably in New York, and ultimately from the German for person.
A [[from:Yiddish]] word that spread from New York slang.
A [[from:Yiddish]] word that spread from New York slang.
A [[from:Yiddish]] word that spread from New York slang; garbled in the captions.
